description: I am an independent researcher and aspiring mechanical engineer driven by a passion for space exploration and structural design. As a solo participant, I combine months of conceptual planning, physics principles, and NASA satellite data to design practical, data-driven solutions for deep space habitats and planetary missions
summary:
Rehearsal Earth is an interactive engineering atlas that asks: where on Earth can we rehearse the Moon and Mars, and how far can we trust it? Using NASA data (MODIS land surface temperature, SRTM elevation, LRO LOLA topography and Diviner temperatures), we compare five Earth sites with a lunar south-pole reference, Malapert massif, and with Mars. Instead of ranking lookalikes, we translate the data into engineering terms: temperature swing, slope, roughness, ground pressure and fall time under different gravity.

Key finding is honest: even the best Earth site reproduces only 7.9% of the Moon’s day–night temperature swing, and all 16 scored comparisons are weak, though Mauna Kea’s terrain comes closest (13.9° against 17.8° median slope). Mission Match shows which site is the best stand-in for a given task, a rover calculator and Gravity Drop show what Earth cannot test, and every number is traceable in a Sources view. Limits are stated openly: five sites, one lunar site, and no radiation or vacuum.
details:
What it does
Rehearsal Earth is a web atlas that answers one question: where on Earth can we rehearse the Moon and Mars, and how far can we trust that rehearsal? Engineers test rovers, landers and habitats at Earth “analog” sites before they fly, but these sites are often chosen because they look right. The atlas measures five well-known analogs (Mauna Kea, Atacama Desert, Altiplano, Haughton Crater and the McMurdo Dry Valleys) against the Moon’s Malapert massif near the south pole and against Mars. It compares them factor by factor: day–night temperature swing, mean temperature, terrain slope and roughness, and gravity.

How it works
A Python pipeline processes NASA data and scores each site with one transparent formula: score = max(0, 1 − |x_Earth − x_ref| / τ), where τ is the tolerance for each factor. A score of 0.8 or more is a strong match, 0.5 or more is partial, and anything lower is weak. The website has seven stations: Thermal, Terrain, Try it (a rover calculator for ground pressure and beam thermal expansion), Gravity Drop, Mission Match (pick a task, get the best Earth stand-in), Validation and Sources. Every number links to its source.

Key findings
The best Earth site, Mauna Kea, reaches only 7.9% of the Moon’s day–night temperature swing. The steepest Earth terrain has a median slope of 13.94°, compared with 17.81° at Malapert. All 16 of 16 scored comparisons are weak. That isn’t a failure: it tells engineers exactly what each site can and cannot rehearse.

Benefits and intended impact
Mission engineers and analog campaign planners can see which site fits which test before spending money on fieldwork. They also see where Earth tests mislead. For example, a 200 kg rover presses 6.1 times harder on Earth soil than on the Moon, so Earth soil tests overstate wheel sinkage. Teachers and students get a hands-on, honest way to explore why the Moon and Mars are so hard to copy on Earth.

Tools and data

  • Data: NASA LRO Diviner and LOLA, MODIS MOD11A2 land surface temperature (via AppEEARS), SRTM 30 m elevation, NASA planetary fact sheets, NASA GIBS map tiles, and NIST material properties.
  • Code: Python (rasterio, numpy, earthaccess, pytest), with HTML, CSS and JavaScript (Leaflet, Chart.js) for the website.
  • Hardware and hosting: a laptop, with the site published on GitHub Pages.
  • AI: the AI assistant Claude helped with coding and writing.

Creativity
Most analog maps show where Earth looks like space. This one measures how much of space each place really reproduces, and it states where the analogy breaks. Interactive stations such as Gravity Drop, the rover calculator and Mission Match turn the numbers into decisions an engineer would actually make.

Factors considered

  • Scientific honesty: benchmarks, a negative control, a tolerance sensitivity check, and limits stated openly. No Earth site has lunar gravity, vacuum or radiation, the Moon’s swing is a NASA reference value, only one Moon terrain site is used, and SRTM covers only 60°N–56°S.
  • Clarity for non-experts: details are hidden behind “Show the numbers”.
  • Room to grow: more Moon sites, Mars terrain, lava tubes and a dryness metric.

Made for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.
